description: Team ShadowTrace is a group of passionate people working to make lunar mission planning simpler. Our team combines backgrounds in renewable energy, programming, and design, which helps us connect solar power and battery limits with real lunar lighting conditions and turn them into a clear, easy-to-use tool. We believe good space decisions should not require complex software, so we built ShadowTrace to give planners a simple answer they can trust.
summary:
ShadowTrace is a web tool that helps mission planners choose safe landing sites at the Moon's south pole. Today, the inputs to that decision are spread across separate systems: site location, sunlight, Earth visibility, terrain and landing error. ShadowTrace brings them together in one interface.

The user chooses a spacecraft and its specifications, sets the landing date, mission duration and exact site, and ShadowTrace simulates hundreds of possible touchdowns inside the lander's landing-error margin. Each is checked against real NASA terrain, sunlight and Earth-visibility data. The result is a clear verdict (Suitable, Conditional or Unsuitable) with the reason behind every check.

When a site fails, ShadowTrace suggests better nearby sites or landing dates under the same rules. This turns complex lunar data into a fast, explainable decision, making early landing-site assessment easier for experts and accessible to non-experts.
details:
What it does and how it works:

ShadowTrace turns scattered lunar data into one clear landing decision for the Moon's south pole. The user moves through six stages: choose a spacecraft (Scout, Explorer or Pioneer concept landers, with editable size, solar power, battery, slope limit and landing accuracy), define the mission (landing date, duration, and one of 13 NASA Artemis III candidate regions or custom coordinates from 75°S to the pole), watch the arrival, inspect the landing zone, get the decision, and compare alternatives.

At the landing zone, ShadowTrace simulates hundreds of touchdowns inside the lander's landing-error ellipse and checks each one against NASA LOLA terrain slope. It then checks illumination (longest continuous darkness, from JPL Horizons and the LOLA horizon), battery power over the mission, and Earth line-of-sight for communication.

The result is a clear verdict (Suitable, Conditional or Unsuitable) with the reason behind every check. Example: "Power holds: the battery never drops below 100%; the longest continuous darkness is 0.0 h." It also shows a decision score, the modelled touchdown safety, and data confidence.

Benefits and intended impact:

Mission planners and students get one understandable answer instead of combining terrain, sunlight, Earth visibility and landing-error data from separate tools. When a site fails, ShadowTrace searches up to 100 km around the target and suggests better nearby sites or landing dates under the same rules. The aim is to speed up early-stage landing-site assessment and make it accessible to non-experts.

Creativity:

1) Inverse search: after a rejection, it finds alternative sites and dates that work.

2) Explained decisions: every verdict says why, not just yes or no.

3) Uncertainty-aware: landers never hit the exact target, so we simulate touchdowns across the landing-error ellipse instead of testing a single point.

4) Honest limits: it clearly flags what it cannot assess (boulders smaller than the 40 m terrain grid, thermal environment), and labels the arrival animation as cinematic rather than a computed trajectory.

5) Basic and Expert modes, in English and Arabic.

Tools and technologies:

Web application deployed on Vercel. NASA LRO LOLA terrain, NASA JPL Horizons ephemerides, NASA Moon Trek, NASA SVS lunar imagery, and IAU/USGS planetary names. Super Intelligence tools were used to assist with research, data analysis and code development.

Factors we considered:

Terrain slope versus the lander's tilt limit, landing uncertainty, polar lighting and power, Earth communication gaps, data resolution limits, and keeping results understandable for non-specialists.
